stem: The theory of 'Continental Drift', which proposed that the continents have moved (drifted) over time, was put forward by:
solution: The theory of Continental Drift was put forward by Alfred Wegener (a German meteorologist and geophysicist) in 1912. Wegener proposed that the continents were not fixed but had drifted (moved) across the Earth's surface over geological time — that they had once been joined together and had since drifted apart to their present positions.

stem: According to Wegener's Continental Drift theory, all the continents were once joined together in a single supercontinent called:
solution: According to Wegener, all the continents were once joined together in a single giant supercontinent, which he called Pangaea (meaning 'all earth' or 'all lands'). Pangaea, he proposed, later broke up, and the continents drifted apart to their present positions. Pangaea was surrounded by a single great ocean called Panthalassa.

stem: The single vast ocean that surrounded the supercontinent Pangaea was called:
solution: The single vast ocean that surrounded the supercontinent Pangaea was called Panthalassa (meaning 'all sea/ocean'). As Pangaea later broke up and the continents drifted apart, this great ocean was divided, and the present-day oceans (Atlantic, Pacific, Indian, etc.) took shape. (There was also a sea called the Tethys, which separated the northern and southern parts of Pangaea as it began to break up.)

stem: When Pangaea began to break up, it first split into two large landmasses: a northern one called Laurasia and a southern one called:
solution: When the supercontinent Pangaea began to break up, it first split into two large landmasses: a northern landmass called Laurasia (or Angaraland), which included the present-day North America, Europe, and Asia; and a southern landmass called Gondwana (or Gondwanaland), which included the present-day South America, Africa, Antarctica, Australia, and the Indian subcontinent. These two landmasses (Laurasia in the north and Gondwana in the south), separated by the Tethys Sea, later broke up further into the present continents, which drifted to their current positions. Understanding the split of Pangaea into Laurasia (north) and Gondwana (south) is an important point. Pangaea first split into Laurasia (north) and Gondwana (south).

stem: Which of the following was a piece of evidence Wegener used to support his Continental Drift theory?
options: The matching ('jig-saw fit') of the coastlines of continents (like South America and Africa), and matching rock formations, fossils, and past climate evidence across now-separated continents
solution: Wegener used several lines of evidence to support his Continental Drift theory, including: the remarkable matching or 'jig-saw fit' of the coastlines of continents on either side of the oceans (for example, the way the east coast of South America seems to fit into the west coast of Africa, as if they were once joined); the matching of rock formations, geological structures, and mountain ranges across now-separated continents; the finding of similar/identical fossils of the same land plants and animals on continents now separated by wide oceans (which would have been impossible if the continents had always been separated, but makes sense if they were once joined); and evidence of past climates (such as signs of ancient glaciation in areas now in warm regions, and coal deposits in cold regions) that only make sense if the continents were once in different positions and joined together. These pieces of evidence (the fit of the coastlines, matching rocks and fossils, and past climate evidence) supported Wegener's idea that the continents were once joined and have since drifted apart. Understanding the evidence for continental drift is an important point. Evidence included the fit of the coastlines, matching rocks and fossils, and past climate evidence.

stem: A major weakness of Wegener's Continental Drift theory (why it was initially not widely accepted) was that:
options: He could not adequately explain the force or mechanism that caused the continents to drift/move
solution: A major weakness of Wegener's Continental Drift theory — and the main reason it was initially not widely accepted by the scientific community — was that Wegener could not adequately explain the force or mechanism that could cause the huge, solid continents to drift (move) across the Earth's surface. Although he presented strong evidence that the continents had once been joined and had drifted apart, the forces he suggested (like tidal forces or forces related to the Earth's rotation) were shown to be far too weak to move the continents, and he could not provide a convincing mechanism for continental drift. This lack of a convincing mechanism led most scientists at the time to reject or ignore his theory. (It was only later, with the development of the ideas of sea-floor spreading and plate tectonics, that a convincing mechanism for the movement of the continents was found, and the essential idea of continental drift was vindicated.) Understanding the main weakness of Wegener's theory (the lack of a convincing mechanism) is an important point. Wegener could not adequately explain the mechanism/force that moved the continents.

stem: The concept that new oceanic crust is created at mid-ocean ridges (where the sea floor spreads apart) is called:
solution: The concept of 'sea-floor spreading' (proposed by Harry Hess in the 1960s) holds that new oceanic crust is continuously being created at the mid-ocean ridges (long undersea mountain ranges/ridges running through the oceans) — where molten material (magma) rises up from the mantle, erupts, and solidifies to form new oceanic crust, pushing the older crust apart on either side. Thus, at the mid-ocean ridges, the sea floor 'spreads' apart as new crust is added, and the ocean widens over time. Sea-floor spreading was a crucial concept that helped explain the movement of the continents (they move as part of the spreading sea floor/plates) and provided the mechanism that Wegener's continental drift theory had lacked. Understanding sea-floor spreading (new oceanic crust created at mid-ocean ridges, spreading the sea floor apart) is an important point. Sea-floor spreading is the creation of new oceanic crust at mid-ocean ridges, spreading the sea floor apart.

stem: The scientist who proposed the concept of sea-floor spreading was:
solution: The concept of sea-floor spreading was proposed by Harry Hess (an American geologist) in the early 1960s. Hess proposed that new oceanic crust is created at the mid-ocean ridges (where magma rises and solidifies), spreading the sea floor apart, and that the older crust eventually descends back into the mantle at the deep ocean trenches (subduction). This concept of sea-floor spreading provided a key part of the mechanism for the movement of the continents and the ocean floors, and it was a major step towards the theory of plate tectonics. Understanding that Harry Hess proposed sea-floor spreading is a point. Harry Hess proposed the concept of sea-floor spreading.

stem: The long, underwater mountain ranges/ridges running through the oceans, where new oceanic crust is formed (sea-floor spreading), are called:
solution: The mid-ocean ridges are the long, continuous underwater mountain ranges or ridges that run through the world's oceans (for example, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge running down the middle of the Atlantic Ocean). At the mid-ocean ridges, molten material (magma) rises up from the mantle, erupts, and solidifies to form new oceanic crust, causing the sea floor to spread apart on either side (sea-floor spreading). The mid-ocean ridges are thus the sites where new oceanic crust is created and the sea floor spreads. (They are divergent plate boundaries, where plates move apart.) Understanding the mid-ocean ridges (where new crust forms and the sea floor spreads) is an important point. Mid-ocean ridges are underwater ridges where new oceanic crust forms (sea-floor spreading).

stem: The deep, narrow depressions in the ocean floor (the deepest parts of the oceans), where old oceanic crust descends/sinks back into the mantle, are called:
solution: Ocean trenches (or deep-sea trenches) are the deep, narrow, elongated depressions in the ocean floor — the deepest parts of the oceans (for example, the Mariana Trench in the Pacific, the deepest place on Earth). At the ocean trenches, old oceanic crust (of one plate) descends or sinks back down into the mantle — a process called subduction — as it collides with and is pushed beneath another plate. Thus, the ocean trenches are the sites where old oceanic crust is destroyed (subducted back into the mantle), balancing the creation of new crust at the mid-ocean ridges. (Ocean trenches are convergent plate boundaries, where plates come together and one is subducted.) Understanding the ocean trenches (where old crust subducts into the mantle) is an important point. Ocean trenches are deep depressions where old oceanic crust subducts back into the mantle.

stem: The process by which one tectonic plate (usually denser oceanic crust) is forced down and sinks beneath another plate into the mantle (at a convergent boundary/trench) is called:
solution: Subduction is the process by which one tectonic plate — usually the denser one (typically oceanic crust) — is forced down and sinks (descends) beneath another plate, down into the mantle, where it is eventually melted and reabsorbed. Subduction occurs at convergent plate boundaries (where plates move towards and collide with each other), and it is associated with the deep ocean trenches (which mark where the plate descends). Subduction is important: it destroys old oceanic crust (balancing the creation of new crust at the ridges), and it is associated with earthquakes, volcanoes, and mountain building at the convergent boundaries. Understanding subduction (one plate sinking beneath another into the mantle at a convergent boundary) is an important point. Subduction is the sinking of one plate beneath another into the mantle at a convergent boundary.

stem: The modern theory that explains the movement of the continents and ocean floors in terms of the movement of large rigid plates of the lithosphere is called:
solution: The theory of Plate Tectonics is the modern, comprehensive theory that explains the movement of the continents and ocean floors, and many of the major features and phenomena of the Earth, in terms of the movement and interaction of large, rigid plates of the lithosphere (tectonic plates). Plate tectonics (developed in the 1960s, building on continental drift and sea-floor spreading) holds that the Earth's lithosphere is broken into a number of rigid plates, which move about (slowly) on the plastic asthenosphere beneath them (driven by convection currents in the mantle), and that the movement and interaction of these plates at their boundaries produces continental drift, the creation and destruction of ocean floors, mountain building, earthquakes, volcanoes, and other major features and phenomena. Plate tectonics is the unifying, widely-accepted theory of the large-scale dynamics of the Earth's surface, incorporating and explaining the earlier ideas of continental drift and sea-floor spreading. Understanding plate tectonics as the modern unifying theory is a key point. Plate tectonics explains the movement of the continents and ocean floors through the movement of lithospheric plates.

stem: According to plate tectonics, the lithosphere is broken into several major and minor:
solution: According to the theory of plate tectonics, the Earth's lithosphere (the rigid outer shell of crust and uppermost mantle) is broken into several large (major) and smaller (minor) rigid pieces called tectonic plates (or lithospheric plates). These plates carry the continents and/or ocean floors, and they move about slowly (a few centimetres per year) on the plastic asthenosphere beneath them. The interaction of these plates at their boundaries (moving apart, colliding, or sliding past one another) produces the major features and phenomena of the Earth. There are about seven major plates (such as the Pacific, North American, South American, Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian, and Antarctic plates) and several minor plates. Understanding that the lithosphere is broken into major and minor tectonic plates is fundamental to plate tectonics. The lithosphere is broken into major and minor tectonic plates.

stem: The plates move because of __________ currents in the mantle (driven by the Earth's internal heat).
solution: The tectonic plates move (drift) because of convection currents in the mantle — slow, circulating flows of the hot, plastic mantle material, driven by the Earth's internal heat. The heat from the Earth's interior causes the material in the mantle (asthenosphere) to circulate in convection currents (hot material rising, cooling, spreading, and sinking again). These slow-moving convection currents in the mantle drag and push the rigid lithospheric plates above them, causing the plates to move (and thus causing sea-floor spreading, continental drift, and plate interactions). Thus, convection currents in the mantle (driven by the Earth's internal heat) are the main driving force behind the movement of the tectonic plates. Understanding that convection currents in the mantle drive plate movement is an important point (this provided the mechanism that Wegener's theory had lacked). Convection currents in the mantle drive the movement of the tectonic plates.

stem: A boundary where two tectonic plates move away from each other (and new crust is created) is called a:
solution: A divergent boundary (or constructive/divergent plate boundary) is a boundary where two tectonic plates move away from (diverge from) each other. As the plates move apart, magma rises up from the mantle to fill the gap and solidifies, creating new crust (this is what happens at the mid-ocean ridges — sea-floor spreading). Divergent boundaries are thus sites where new crust is created and the plates move apart (also called constructive boundaries, as new crust is constructed). (Examples include the mid-ocean ridges, like the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.) Understanding the divergent boundary (plates moving apart, new crust created) is an important type of plate boundary. A divergent boundary is where plates move apart and new crust is created.

stem: A boundary where two tectonic plates move towards each other (and crust may be destroyed by subduction, or mountains formed) is called a:
solution: A convergent boundary (or destructive/convergent plate boundary) is a boundary where two tectonic plates move towards (converge on) each other and collide. At convergent boundaries, various things can happen depending on the types of plates involved: one plate (usually the denser oceanic plate) may be subducted (forced down beneath the other into the mantle, destroying crust — hence 'destructive' boundary — and forming deep ocean trenches, volcanoes, and earthquakes); or two continental plates may collide and crumple up, forming great fold mountains (like the Himalayas). Thus, convergent boundaries are sites where plates collide, and crust may be destroyed (by subduction) or mountains may be formed. Understanding the convergent boundary (plates moving together, subduction or mountain building) is an important type of plate boundary. A convergent boundary is where plates move towards each other, with subduction or mountain building.

stem: A boundary where two tectonic plates slide past each other horizontally (without creating or destroying crust) is called a:
solution: A transform boundary (or transform fault boundary, also called a conservative boundary) is a boundary where two tectonic plates slide past each other horizontally (in opposite directions, or at different speeds), without either creating new crust or destroying old crust (hence 'conservative' — crust is neither created nor destroyed). The plates grind past each other along a transform fault, and this movement is often not smooth but jerky (the plates lock and then suddenly slip), causing earthquakes. (A famous example is the San Andreas Fault in California, where the Pacific and North American plates slide past each other.) Understanding the transform boundary (plates sliding past each other, causing earthquakes, without creating or destroying crust) is an important type of plate boundary. A transform boundary is where plates slide past each other horizontally, causing earthquakes.

stem: The Himalayan mountains were formed by the collision of the Indian plate with the:
solution: The Himalayan mountains (the great fold mountains along India's northern border) were formed by the collision of the Indian plate (carrying the Indian subcontinent) with the Eurasian plate. As the Indian plate (which had drifted northward after breaking away from Gondwana) collided with the Eurasian plate, the intervening Tethys Sea was closed, and the crust at the boundary was crumpled, folded, and uplifted to form the great Himalayan mountain ranges (a process of continent-continent collision at a convergent boundary). The Himalayas are thus a classic example of fold mountains formed by the collision of two continental plates (the Indian and Eurasian plates), and this collision is still continuing (the Indian plate is still moving northward, and the Himalayas are still rising). Understanding that the Himalayas were formed by the collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates is an important and prelims-relevant point. The Himalayas were formed by the collision of the Indian plate with the Eurasian plate.

stem: The theory of plate tectonics successfully explains many major Earth phenomena, including:
options: The distribution of continents and oceans, mountain building, the distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes (along plate boundaries), and continental drift
solution: The theory of plate tectonics successfully explains a wide range of major features and phenomena of the Earth, including: the distribution and movement of the continents and oceans (continental drift, and the creation and destruction of ocean floors); the building of mountains (fold mountains formed by plate collisions, like the Himalayas); the distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes (which are concentrated along the plate boundaries, where the plates interact); the formation of ocean ridges and trenches; and many other large-scale features and processes of the Earth's surface. By explaining all these phenomena in terms of the movement and interaction of the tectonic plates, plate tectonics provides a powerful, unifying theory of the large-scale dynamics and features of the Earth. Understanding that plate tectonics explains the distribution of continents and oceans, mountain building, and the distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes is an important point. Plate tectonics explains continental drift, mountain building, and the distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes.

stem: The largest of the Earth's major tectonic plates is the:
solution: The Pacific plate is the largest of the Earth's major tectonic plates. It underlies most of the Pacific Ocean and is composed almost entirely of oceanic crust. The other major plates include the North American, South American, Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian (or Indian and Australian), and Antarctic plates. The Pacific plate, being the largest, is bordered by many subduction zones and is surrounded by the 'Ring of Fire' of earthquakes and volcanoes. Knowing that the Pacific plate is the largest is a point. The Pacific plate is the largest tectonic plate.

stem: The continental crust is generally much __________ than the oceanic crust in age.
options: Older (the oceanic crust is continually created and destroyed, so it is young, while continental crust is old)
solution: The continental crust is generally much older than the oceanic crust. This is because the oceanic crust is continually being created (at the mid-ocean ridges) and destroyed (subducted at the trenches) — so oceanic crust is constantly being recycled and is relatively young (nowhere older than about 200 million years). The continental crust, by contrast, is not subducted (it is lighter and 'rides' on top), so it is not recycled in the same way and can be very old (some continental rocks are billions of years old). Thus, the oceanic crust is young (continually recycled), while the continental crust is old. Understanding that oceanic crust is young (recycled) and continental crust is old is an important point (and evidence for sea-floor spreading and plate tectonics). Continental crust is much older than oceanic crust (which is young, being continually recycled).

stem: The age of the oceanic crust __________ with distance away from the mid-ocean ridge.
options: Increases (the crust is youngest at the ridge and gets older farther away)
solution: The age of the oceanic crust increases with distance away from the mid-ocean ridge. Since new oceanic crust is created at the mid-ocean ridge (and then moves away from the ridge as more new crust is created behind it), the crust is youngest right at the ridge, and it gets progressively older the farther away from the ridge it is (having been created earlier and moved away). This pattern — the oceanic crust being youngest at the ridge and getting older with distance from the ridge (and roughly symmetrical on both sides of the ridge) — is a key piece of evidence for sea-floor spreading and plate tectonics (it shows that new crust is being created at the ridge and spreading outward). Understanding that the age of the oceanic crust increases away from the ridge is an important point (and evidence for sea-floor spreading). The age of the oceanic crust increases with distance from the mid-ocean ridge.

stem: The pattern of magnetic 'stripes' (alternating normal and reversed magnetism) in the rocks of the ocean floor, symmetrical on both sides of the mid-ocean ridge, is evidence for:
options: Sea-floor spreading (the new crust records the Earth's magnetic field, which reverses over time, as it forms and moves away from the ridge)
solution: The pattern of magnetic 'stripes' — alternating bands of normal and reversed magnetic polarity — found in the rocks of the ocean floor, running parallel to the mid-ocean ridge and symmetrical (matching) on both sides of it, is important evidence for sea-floor spreading (this is 'palaeomagnetism'). As new oceanic crust forms at the ridge (from cooling magma), it records the direction of the Earth's magnetic field at the time it forms (the magnetic minerals aligning with the field). Since the Earth's magnetic field reverses (flips) its polarity at intervals over geological time, the crust formed at different times records different (normal or reversed) polarities. As the crust forms at the ridge and spreads away on both sides, it creates a symmetrical pattern of magnetic stripes (of alternating polarity) recording the history of the Earth's magnetic reversals — with matching patterns on both sides of the ridge. This symmetrical pattern of magnetic stripes on the ocean floor is strong evidence that new crust is created at the ridge and spreads away symmetrically on both sides (sea-floor spreading), and it was crucial in confirming sea-floor spreading and plate tectonics. Understanding the magnetic stripes as evidence for sea-floor spreading is an important point. The symmetrical magnetic stripes on the ocean floor are evidence for sea-floor spreading.

stem: Which of the following fossils/plants provided evidence for continental drift (being found on now-separated southern continents that were once joined in Gondwana)?
options: The fern-like plant Glossopteris and the reptile Mesosaurus
solution: Evidence for continental drift came from the finding of identical fossils of certain ancient plants and animals on continents now separated by wide oceans, which were once joined together in Gondwana. Examples include: the fossils of Glossopteris (an ancient fern-like plant/seed fern) found across the now-separated southern continents (South America, Africa, India, Antarctica, Australia); and the fossils of Mesosaurus (a small freshwater/coastal reptile) found in both South America and Africa (but nowhere else). Since these plants and animals could not have crossed the wide oceans that now separate these continents, their presence on now-separated continents makes sense only if those continents were once joined together (in Gondwana) when these organisms lived, and have since drifted apart. Thus, the matching fossils (like Glossopteris and Mesosaurus) on now-separated continents provided important evidence for continental drift and for the former existence of Gondwana. Understanding this fossil evidence for continental drift is an important point. Fossils like Glossopteris (a plant) and Mesosaurus (a reptile), found on now-separated continents, provided evidence for continental drift.

stem: The Indian plate, after breaking away from Gondwana, drifted rapidly __________ before colliding with the Eurasian plate.
solution: After breaking away from the southern supercontinent Gondwana, the Indian plate (carrying the Indian subcontinent) drifted rapidly northward — moving across the Tethys Sea towards the Eurasian plate — over millions of years, before eventually colliding with the Eurasian plate (a collision that formed the Himalayas and is still continuing). The northward drift of the Indian plate is a notable feature of the movement of the continents, and its collision with Eurasia formed the Himalayas and the Tibetan plateau. During its northward journey, the Indian plate is also thought to have passed over a volcanic hotspot, which produced the massive volcanic eruptions that formed the Deccan Traps (the extensive basalt lava plateaus of the Deccan). Understanding that the Indian plate drifted northward (colliding with Eurasia to form the Himalayas) is an important and prelims-relevant point. The Indian plate drifted northward before colliding with the Eurasian plate.

stem: The extensive basalt lava plateaus of peninsular India (the Deccan Traps) are thought to have formed when the drifting Indian plate passed over a:
options: Volcanic 'hotspot' (a plume of hot material from the mantle), causing massive volcanic eruptions
solution: The extensive basalt lava plateaus of peninsular India — the Deccan Traps (vast layers of basalt formed from massive volcanic lava flows) — are thought to have formed when the drifting Indian plate passed over a volcanic 'hotspot' (a fixed plume of hot material rising from deep in the mantle), around 65 million years ago. As the Indian plate moved over this hotspot (the Reunion hotspot), the intense volcanic activity produced enormous outpourings of basaltic lava, which spread over a vast area and solidified to form the extensive basalt layers of the Deccan Traps. (These massive eruptions are also sometimes linked to the extinction of the dinosaurs.) Thus, the Deccan Traps formed from massive volcanic eruptions as the Indian plate passed over a hotspot. Understanding the origin of the Deccan Traps (from a hotspot during the Indian plate's drift) is an important and prelims-relevant point. The Deccan Traps formed from massive volcanic eruptions as the Indian plate passed over a hotspot.

stem: A 'hotspot' in plate tectonics is:
options: A fixed area of intense volcanic activity, fed by a plume of hot material rising from deep in the mantle, over which plates move (creating chains of volcanoes, like Hawaii)
solution: A 'hotspot' in plate tectonics is a fixed area (location) of intense, persistent volcanic activity, fed by a 'plume' of unusually hot material rising from deep within the mantle. Hotspots are relatively fixed in position (staying in roughly the same place in the mantle), while the tectonic plates move over them. As a plate moves over a fixed hotspot, the hotspot's volcanic activity creates a chain or line of volcanoes on the plate — with the volcano currently over the hotspot being active, and the older volcanoes (which have moved off the hotspot) becoming extinct and progressively older along the chain. (The Hawaiian Islands are a famous example — a chain of volcanic islands created as the Pacific plate moved over the Hawaiian hotspot. The Deccan Traps are linked to the Reunion hotspot.) Understanding what a hotspot is (a fixed area of volcanic activity from a mantle plume, over which plates move) is an important point. A hotspot is a fixed area of volcanic activity from a mantle plume, over which plates move, creating volcano chains.

stem: The Hawaiian Islands are a chain of volcanic islands formed as the Pacific plate moved over a:
solution: The Hawaiian Islands are a famous chain of volcanic islands formed as the Pacific plate moved (northwestward) over a fixed volcanic hotspot (the Hawaiian hotspot). As the Pacific plate moved over the fixed hotspot, the hotspot's volcanic activity created a succession of volcanic islands: the island currently over the hotspot (the 'Big Island' of Hawaii) has active volcanoes, while the older islands (which formed earlier over the hotspot and have since moved away with the plate) become progressively older and more eroded (and eventually extinct) along the chain to the northwest. The Hawaiian Islands are thus a classic example of a hotspot volcano chain, illustrating both the existence of hotspots and the movement of the (Pacific) plate over the fixed hotspot. Understanding that the Hawaiian Islands formed as the Pacific plate moved over a hotspot is an important point. The Hawaiian Islands formed as the Pacific plate moved over a hotspot.

stem: The mid-ocean ridge system, running through all the world's oceans, is significant as:
options: The longest mountain chain/range on Earth (though mostly underwater)
solution: The mid-ocean ridge system — the connected system of mid-ocean ridges running through all the world's major oceans (the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, the East Pacific Rise, the ridges of the Indian Ocean, etc.) — is significant as the longest mountain chain/range on Earth, though it is mostly hidden underwater (beneath the oceans). This globe-encircling system of undersea mountain ridges, stretching for tens of thousands of kilometres through the oceans, is where new oceanic crust is continually being created (sea-floor spreading) at the divergent plate boundaries. The fact that the mid-ocean ridge system is the longest mountain range on Earth (mostly underwater) is a notable point, and it reflects the extent and importance of the sea-floor spreading process. Understanding that the mid-ocean ridge system is the longest mountain range on Earth (mostly underwater) is a point. The mid-ocean ridge system is the longest mountain chain on Earth, mostly underwater.

stem: The three types of convergent (collision) plate boundaries are: ocean-ocean, ocean-continent, and:
solution: There are three types of convergent (collision) plate boundaries, depending on the types of plates (crust) that are colliding: (1) ocean-ocean convergence (two oceanic plates collide; one is subducted beneath the other, forming a deep trench and a chain of volcanic islands — an 'island arc'); (2) ocean-continent convergence (an oceanic plate collides with a continental plate; the denser oceanic plate is subducted beneath the continental plate, forming a trench and coastal mountains/volcanoes — like the Andes); and (3) continent-continent convergence (two continental plates collide; since both are light and neither is easily subducted, the crust crumples and is uplifted to form great fold mountains — like the Himalayas). Thus, the three types of convergent boundaries are ocean-ocean, ocean-continent, and continent-continent. Understanding the three types of convergent boundaries and their results is an important point. The three types of convergent boundaries are ocean-ocean, ocean-continent, and continent-continent.

stem: A continent-continent collision (like the Indian and Eurasian plates) results in the formation of:
options: Great fold mountains (like the Himalayas), as the crust crumples and is uplifted
solution: A continent-continent collision (where two continental plates collide, as in the collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates) results in the formation of great fold mountains. Because both colliding plates carry light continental crust (which is not easily subducted into the mantle), when they collide, the crust at the boundary is crumpled, folded, and pushed up (uplifted), forming great fold mountain ranges. The Himalayas (formed by the collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates) are the classic example of fold mountains formed by continent-continent collision. Thus, continent-continent collisions produce great fold mountains. Understanding that continent-continent collision forms great fold mountains (like the Himalayas) is an important point. Continent-continent collision forms great fold mountains, like the Himalayas.

stem: The East African Rift Valley is an example of a __________ boundary, where the continent is being pulled apart.
options: Divergent (a place where a continent is rifting/splitting apart)
solution: The East African Rift Valley is an example of a divergent boundary occurring within a continent — a place where the continental crust (of Africa) is being pulled apart (rifting/splitting) as tectonic forces (a divergent boundary/rifting) begin to tear the continent apart. At the East African Rift, the crust is being stretched and thinned, forming a long rift valley (a down-dropped block bounded by faults), with associated volcanic activity and earthquakes. This rifting represents an early stage of continental splitting — if it continues, it could eventually split Africa apart and form a new ocean (as happened when other continents rifted and split in the past). The East African Rift Valley is thus an example of a divergent (rifting) boundary within a continent, where the continent is being pulled apart. Understanding the East African Rift Valley as a divergent/rifting boundary is a point. The East African Rift Valley is a divergent boundary where the continent is being pulled apart.

stem: The movement of tectonic plates is very slow, at a rate of about:
options: A few centimetres per year (comparable to the growth of fingernails)
solution: The movement of the tectonic plates is very slow — at a rate of only about a few centimetres per year (typically around 1 to 10 cm per year, roughly comparable to the rate at which human fingernails grow). Although this rate is tiny on a human timescale, over the vast spans of geological time (millions and hundreds of millions of years), this slow movement adds up to enormous distances — enough to move the continents thousands of kilometres, open and close oceans, and build mountain ranges. Modern techniques (like GPS) can actually measure this slow movement of the plates directly. Understanding that the plates move very slowly (a few cm per year), but that this adds up to great changes over geological time, is an important point. The tectonic plates move very slowly, at about a few centimetres per year.

stem: The evidence of ancient glaciation (glacial deposits/tillite) found in areas now located in warm tropical regions (like India, Africa, South America) supports continental drift because it suggests:
options: These areas were once located near the South Pole (in Gondwana), where they were glaciated, before drifting to their present warm positions
Glaciers can form in the tropics today
solution: The evidence of ancient glaciation — such as glacial deposits (tillite) and marks of past ice sheets — found in areas now located in warm, tropical, or temperate regions (like India, Africa, South America, and Australia) supports continental drift, because it suggests that these areas were once located in a much colder region (near the South Pole) where they were covered by ice sheets and glaciated. This makes sense if these now-separated southern continents were once joined together in Gondwana, positioned near the South Pole (where they were glaciated), and have since drifted apart and moved to their present, warmer positions. (Glaciers could not form in these areas in their present warm tropical positions, so the evidence of past glaciation shows they must have been elsewhere — near the pole — in the past.) Thus, the evidence of ancient glaciation in now-warm areas supports continental drift and the former existence of Gondwana near the South Pole. Understanding this past-climate (glaciation) evidence for continental drift is an important point. Ancient glaciation evidence in now-warm areas supports continental drift (these areas were once near the South Pole in Gondwana).

stem: The continental margin includes the gently-sloping, shallow, submerged edge of the continent (rich in resources), called the:
solution: The continental shelf is the gently-sloping, shallow, submerged edge (extension) of a continent — the part of the continental margin that lies under the shallow water bordering the continents. The continental shelf is shallow (typically less than 200 m deep), gently sloping, and it can be rich in resources (it is important for fishing — as sunlight reaches the shallow water, supporting abundant marine life — and it can contain deposits of oil, natural gas, and minerals). Beyond the continental shelf, the sea floor drops off more steeply (the continental slope) into the deep ocean. The continental shelf is an important part of the ocean floor relief and of the continental margin. Understanding the continental shelf (the shallow, gently-sloping, resource-rich submerged edge of the continent) is a point. The continental shelf is the shallow, gently-sloping submerged edge of the continent, rich in resources.

stem: The vast, flat, deep regions of the ocean floor (the deep sea bed) are called the:
solution: The abyssal plains are the vast, flat (or very gently undulating), deep regions of the ocean floor — the deep sea bed that covers large parts of the ocean floor (at great depths, typically 3,000-6,000 m). The abyssal plains are among the flattest and smoothest regions on Earth, formed largely by the accumulation of fine sediments over the deep ocean floor. They are an important feature of the ocean floor relief, lying between the continental margins and the mid-ocean ridges. Understanding the abyssal plains (the vast, flat, deep regions of the ocean floor) is a point about ocean floor relief. The abyssal plains are the vast, flat, deep regions of the ocean floor.

stem: The point on the Earth's surface from which continental drift and plate tectonics ultimately derive their driving energy is the Earth's:
solution: The ultimate driving energy for continental drift and plate tectonics comes from the Earth's internal heat (the heat of the Earth's interior — from the heat left over from its formation and from radioactive decay). This internal heat drives the convection currents in the mantle (the slow circulation of the hot, plastic mantle material), and these mantle convection currents, in turn, drive the movement of the tectonic plates (dragging and pushing the plates), causing sea-floor spreading, subduction, continental drift, and plate interactions. Thus, the Earth's internal heat is the ultimate source of energy that drives plate tectonics and the movement of the continents. (This is distinct from the Sun's energy, which drives the external/exogenic processes like weathering and erosion, and the atmosphere and oceans.) Understanding that the Earth's internal heat is the driving energy for plate tectonics is an important point (linking the interior to the movement of continents). The Earth's internal heat drives the convection currents that move the tectonic plates.

stem: Which of the following is a correct sequence in the historical development of the understanding of continental/plate movement?
options: Plate tectonics → sea-floor spreading → continental drift
Continental Drift (Wegener) → Sea-floor spreading (Hess) → Plate Tectonics
Sea-floor spreading → continental drift → plate tectonics
solution: The correct historical sequence in the development of the understanding of continental/plate movement is: (1) Continental Drift theory (Alfred Wegener, 1912) — which proposed that the continents had drifted apart from a former supercontinent (Pangaea), but lacked a convincing mechanism; (2) Sea-floor Spreading (Harry Hess, 1960s) — which proposed the creation of new oceanic crust at mid-ocean ridges and provided a mechanism for the movement of the continents/ocean floors; and (3) Plate Tectonics (developed in the 1960s) — the modern, unifying theory that incorporated and built upon continental drift and sea-floor spreading, explaining the movement of the lithospheric plates and the major features and phenomena of the Earth. Thus, the sequence is: Continental Drift → Sea-floor Spreading → Plate Tectonics. Understanding this historical development (from continental drift, through sea-floor spreading, to plate tectonics) is an important point. The sequence was Continental Drift (Wegener) → Sea-floor Spreading (Hess) → Plate Tectonics.

stem: The essential idea of Wegener's continental drift was ultimately __________ by the later theory of plate tectonics.
options: Vindicated/confirmed (the continents do move, though as part of plates, driven by mantle convection — providing the mechanism Wegener had lacked)
solution: The essential idea of Wegener's continental drift — that the continents move (drift) over time, and were once joined together — was ultimately vindicated (confirmed) by the later theory of plate tectonics. Although Wegener's theory had been rejected in his own time because he could not explain the mechanism, the later development of sea-floor spreading and plate tectonics showed that the continents do indeed move — as part of the larger tectonic plates, which move due to convection currents in the mantle. Thus, plate tectonics provided the mechanism that Wegener had lacked, and it confirmed and incorporated the essential idea of continental drift (that the continents move and were once joined), while explaining it in the fuller framework of plate movement. Wegener's basic insight was therefore vindicated and is now accepted (within the framework of plate tectonics). Understanding that Wegener's continental drift was ultimately vindicated by plate tectonics is an important point about the development of science. Wegener's continental drift was ultimately vindicated by plate tectonics, which provided the mechanism.

stem: Which of the following correctly matches a plate boundary type with a feature it produces?
options: Divergent boundary — mid-ocean ridges (new crust); Convergent boundary — trenches/mountains (crust destroyed or uplifted); Transform boundary — earthquakes (crust conserved)
solution: The correct matches are: Divergent boundaries produce mid-ocean ridges (where plates move apart and new crust is created — 'constructive'); Convergent boundaries produce ocean trenches (where crust is subducted/destroyed — 'destructive') and/or fold mountains (where continents collide and crust is uplifted); and Transform boundaries produce earthquakes (where plates slide past each other, and crust is neither created nor destroyed — 'conservative'). Knowing which features each type of plate boundary produces — divergent (mid-ocean ridges, new crust), convergent (trenches, mountains, crust destroyed/uplifted), transform (earthquakes, crust conserved) — is an important point. Divergent boundaries make mid-ocean ridges (new crust), convergent boundaries make trenches/mountains, and transform boundaries cause earthquakes.

stem: Volcanic island arcs (chains of volcanic islands, like Japan or Indonesia) are formed at:
options: Convergent (ocean-ocean subduction) boundaries, where one oceanic plate is subducted beneath another
solution: Volcanic island arcs — curved chains of volcanic islands (such as Japan, the Philippines, Indonesia, and the Aleutian Islands) — are formed at convergent boundaries where one oceanic plate is subducted beneath another oceanic plate (ocean-ocean convergence). As the subducting oceanic plate descends into the mantle, it causes melting and the rise of magma, which erupts to form a chain (arc) of volcanic islands on the overriding plate, parallel to the deep ocean trench that marks the subduction zone. Thus, volcanic island arcs form at ocean-ocean convergent (subduction) boundaries. Understanding that volcanic island arcs form at ocean-ocean subduction (convergent) boundaries is a point. Volcanic island arcs form at ocean-ocean convergent (subduction) boundaries.

stem: The Andes mountains (along the western edge of South America) were formed by:
options: The subduction of an oceanic plate (the Nazca plate) beneath the continental South American plate (ocean-continent convergence)
solution: The Andes mountains (the great mountain range running along the western edge of South America) were formed by ocean-continent convergence — the subduction of an oceanic plate (the Nazca plate) beneath the continental South American plate. As the denser oceanic Nazca plate is subducted (forced down) beneath the western edge of the South American continent, the process causes the uplift, folding, and volcanic activity that built the Andes mountains (with associated volcanoes, earthquakes, and a deep ocean trench offshore). The Andes are thus a classic example of mountains formed at an ocean-continent convergent (subduction) boundary (in contrast to the Himalayas, formed by continent-continent collision). Understanding that the Andes formed by ocean-continent subduction is a point. The Andes formed by the subduction of the oceanic Nazca plate beneath the continental South American plate.

stem: The Atlantic Ocean is __________ over time due to sea-floor spreading at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
options: Widening (growing wider), as new crust is added at the ridge, pushing the Americas away from Europe/Africa
solution: The Atlantic Ocean is widening (growing wider) over time due to sea-floor spreading at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge (the mid-ocean ridge running down the middle of the Atlantic). At the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, new oceanic crust is continually being created (as magma rises and solidifies), spreading the sea floor apart and pushing the continents on either side — the Americas on one side, and Europe and Africa on the other — farther apart. As a result, the Atlantic Ocean is gradually getting wider over time (as the Americas move away from Europe and Africa). (This is a continuation of the process that began when Pangaea broke up and the Atlantic first opened.) Thus, the Atlantic Ocean is widening due to sea-floor spreading at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Understanding that the Atlantic is widening due to sea-floor spreading is a point. The Atlantic Ocean is widening due to sea-floor spreading at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

stem: The distribution of the world's earthquakes and volcanoes is not random but is concentrated:
options: In the centres of the continents
Along the boundaries of the tectonic plates
solution: The distribution of the world's earthquakes and volcanoes is not random but is strongly concentrated along the boundaries of the tectonic plates — the zones where the plates meet and interact (moving apart, colliding, or sliding past one another). It is at these plate boundaries that the stresses, movements, subduction, and magma generation associated with plate interactions occur, producing most of the world's earthquakes and volcanoes. (For example, the 'Ring of Fire' around the Pacific, and the belts of earthquakes and volcanoes along the mid-ocean ridges and the great mountain belts, all follow the plate boundaries.) This concentration of earthquakes and volcanoes along the plate boundaries is a key piece of evidence for plate tectonics, and it links these phenomena to the movement and interaction of the plates. Understanding that earthquakes and volcanoes are concentrated along plate boundaries is an important point. Earthquakes and volcanoes are concentrated along the boundaries of the tectonic plates.

stem: The theory of plate tectonics is important because it provides a __________ explanation for a wide range of Earth phenomena.
options: Unifying (single, comprehensive) explanation — tying together continental drift, ocean floor features, mountain building, earthquakes, and volcanoes
solution: The theory of plate tectonics is important because it provides a unifying (single, comprehensive, and powerful) explanation for a wide range of major Earth phenomena — tying together, within a single framework, phenomena that had previously seemed separate or unexplained. Plate tectonics explains, in a unified way: the movement and distribution of the continents (continental drift); the features and history of the ocean floors (mid-ocean ridges, trenches, sea-floor spreading, the age and magnetic patterns of the ocean crust); the building of mountains (fold mountains from plate collisions); and the distribution and cause of earthquakes and volcanoes (along the plate boundaries). By explaining all these diverse phenomena in terms of the single underlying process of plate movement and interaction, plate tectonics provides a grand, unifying theory of the large-scale dynamics and features of the solid Earth — one of the great achievements of modern earth science (sometimes compared in importance to the theory of evolution in biology). Understanding that plate tectonics provides a unifying explanation for a wide range of Earth phenomena is an important point about its significance. Plate tectonics provides a unifying explanation for continental drift, ocean features, mountain building, earthquakes, and volcanoes.

stem: The seven major plates include the Pacific, North American, South American, Eurasian, African, Antarctic, and the:
solution: The seven major tectonic plates are generally listed as: the Pacific plate, the North American plate, the South American plate, the Eurasian plate, the African plate, the Antarctic plate, and the Indo-Australian plate (which carries the Indian subcontinent and Australia; sometimes the Indian and Australian plates are counted separately). In addition to these seven major plates, there are several minor plates (such as the Nazca, Arabian, Caribbean, Cocos, Philippine, and others). Knowing the seven major plates — including the Indo-Australian plate (which carries India) — is a useful point. The seven major plates include the Pacific, North American, South American, Eurasian, African, Antarctic, and Indo-Australian plates.

stem: The movement of the plates today can be directly measured using:
options: Modern techniques such as GPS (Global Positioning System) and satellite measurements
solution: The very slow movement of the tectonic plates today can actually be directly measured using modern techniques such as GPS (the Global Positioning System) and other satellite-based and precise geodetic measurements. By placing GPS receivers at fixed points on different plates and measuring their positions very precisely over time, scientists can directly detect and measure the slow movement of the plates (of a few centimetres per year) relative to one another. These modern measurements confirm the movement of the plates predicted by plate tectonics, and they provide direct, ongoing evidence of plate motion. Thus, the movement of the plates today is directly measured using GPS and satellite techniques. Understanding that modern techniques (GPS) can directly measure plate movement is an interesting and important point (providing direct confirmation of plate tectonics). Plate movement today is directly measured using GPS and satellite techniques.

stem: The study of the distribution and movement of oceans and continents (plate tectonics) is fundamental to physical geography because it:
options: Is irrelevant to the Earth's surface

Explains the large-scale arrangement and history of the continents and oceans, the building of major landforms (mountains), and the distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes — the foundation for understanding the Earth's surface and its evolution
solution: The study of the distribution and movement of oceans and continents (plate tectonics) is fundamental to physical geography because it explains the large-scale arrangement, movement, and history of the continents and oceans, the building of the major landforms (especially the great mountain ranges), and the distribution of major phenomena like earthquakes and volcanoes — providing the foundation for understanding the structure, features, and evolution of the Earth's surface. Plate tectonics is the grand unifying framework for understanding the dynamic, ever-changing nature of the Earth's surface — how the continents and oceans came to be arranged as they are (and how they continue to move and change), how the major landforms (like mountains) are built, and why earthquakes and volcanoes occur where they do. It thus provides the essential large-scale context and foundation for the study of the Earth's surface, its landforms, and its evolution — central concerns of physical geography (especially geomorphology). Understanding the fundamental importance of plate tectonics for physical geography (as the framework for understanding the arrangement, building, and dynamics of the Earth's surface) illustrates its foundational role. Plate tectonics is fundamental to physical geography, explaining the arrangement and history of continents and oceans, mountain building, and the distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Distribution of Oceans and Continents' is that:
options: The continents and oceans are fixed and have never moved

The distribution of continents and oceans is the result of the movement of the Earth's lithospheric (tectonic) plates over time — from Wegener's continental drift (Pangaea breaking up), through sea-floor spreading, to the unifying theory of plate tectonics, which explains continental movement, ocean formation, mountain building, earthquakes, and volcanoes
Nothing is known about how continents formed
solution: The chapter conveys that the present distribution of the continents and oceans is not fixed or permanent, but is the result of the movement of the Earth's lithospheric (tectonic) plates over geological time. The chapter traces the development of the understanding of this: Alfred Wegener's theory of Continental Drift (1912) proposed that the continents were once joined in a single supercontinent, Pangaea (surrounded by the ocean Panthalassa), which broke up (first into Laurasia in the north and Gondwana in the south) and drifted apart to their present positions — supported by evidence such as the fit of the coastlines, matching rocks and fossils, and past climate evidence, but initially rejected because Wegener could not explain the mechanism. Later, the concept of sea-floor spreading (Harry Hess) — the creation of new oceanic crust at the mid-ocean ridges (spreading the sea floor apart) and its destruction at the ocean trenches (subduction) — provided a mechanism, and led to the modern, unifying theory of Plate Tectonics. According to plate tectonics, the lithosphere is broken into rigid plates that move (driven by convection currents in the mantle) and interact at their boundaries (divergent boundaries, where plates move apart and new crust forms; convergent boundaries, where plates collide, with subduction or mountain building — as in the Himalayas, formed by the collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates; and transform boundaries, where plates slide past each other, causing earthquakes). Plate tectonics thus explains the distribution and movement of continents and oceans, mountain building, and the distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes (concentrated along plate boundaries). Therefore, the distribution of continents and oceans, and many major features and phenomena of the Earth, are the result of the movement and interaction of the tectonic plates over time. Understanding the movement of the continents and oceans through plate tectonics (from continental drift and sea-floor spreading to the unifying theory of plate tectonics) is the central message of the chapter, and it is fundamental to understanding the dynamic, ever-changing nature of the Earth's surface and the forces that shape it.
